title: Edward Worthington at Worthington's Fort
summary: Irish-born surveyor Edward Worthington served under George Rogers Clark at Vincennes, then planted Worthington’s Fort southeast of present Danville.
bodyMarkdown:
[Edward Worthington](/people/#edward-worthington) was born in Ireland around 1754 and reached the Kentucky country young. By 1775 he was surveying on Beargrass Creek, near the Falls of the Ohio, in a land that had no towns yet. He was a hunter, a surveyor, and soon a soldier.

He fought in Lord Dunmore's War. On December 29, 1776, he was wounded defending McClelland's Station, at today's [Georgetown](/stories/georgetown-and-royal-spring/), against Mingo warriors under [Pluggy](/people/#pluggy). Pluggy was killed in that fight, and the settlers soon abandoned the station.

When [George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) led Virginia's Illinois campaign, Worthington went with him as a captain and paymaster. He helped take Vincennes in 1779, when Clark's men forced the British garrison to surrender. Virginia later [granted him 3,234 acres](https://grokipedia.com/page/edward_worthington) for that service.

That same year he planted Worthington's Fort, about four miles southeast of present [Danville](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/). It was one of the small stations that sheltered families in the central Kentucky settlements while the war went on.

In 1780 Clark ordered Worthington's company far to the west. They were to occupy the Chickasaw Bluffs, just below where the Ohio meets the Mississippi, and build Fort Jefferson. The post was meant to guard Virginia's claim to the Illinois country against enemies coming up the river.

The fort stood on Chickasaw land, and the Chickasaw kept up steady pressure on it. Supplies ran short, and in 1781 the garrison abandoned Fort Jefferson. It was one of Clark's few outright failures.

After the war Worthington lived as many veterans did, on land claims and in lawsuits. He died of yellow fever in New Orleans in 1804 while pursuing a land-fraud suit. His family is buried in the Worthington Family Cemetery at Owensboro.

His life traces the whole frontier war in Kentucky, from the first surveys on Beargrass Creek to a station near Danville and a failed fort on the Mississippi.

## Kentucky today

No state marker for Worthington's Fort has been confirmed. The Danville story lives at [Constitution Square](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/), where the district's conventions met. The Fort Jefferson site is remembered at Fort Jefferson Hill near Wickliffe in Ballard County, close to [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/).
Source: [Grokipedia: Edward Worthington](https://grokipedia.com/page/edward_worthington)
